I'd like to see one person one time with injuries that match the alleged method of attack.

A conventional chemical explosion injures by two primary mechanisms: blast overpressure and fragmentation. Most people think of fragmentation wounds from an explosion due to the greater effective range frag has over blast. Nails, ball bearings, and other dense material packed around an explosive, the container itself, and anything that the overpressure can accelerate to high enough speeds all become frag. The fragments travel at high speeds, cause penetrating wounds, and can lead to traumatic amputations.

Blast damage causes fewer casualties mainly due to the fact that increased distance from the detonation causes drastically reduced effects (inverse-square law). Blast injuries can cause immense damage and death even with no fragmentation present. Even exposure to a moderate detonation's blast wave can cause a concussion and disorientation. Eardrums are incredibly susceptible to overpressure damage. Lung tissue can be damaged from the overpressure, causing rupturing of the alveoli and allowing blood into the lungs, causing the victim to cough up blood or pink froth if they're still able to do so. Additionally, flesh can be stripped off of the body and traumatic amputation can occur if the distance to the detonation is close enough.

So why do you see more survivors than killed? The human body does an astonishingly good job at absorbing blast and frag. People very close to the detonation will surely be killed, but the portion of the overpressure that hits them is absorbed by their bodies while fragmentation which hits them is either captured in their flesh or slowed down significantly enough that it has much less kinetic energy and so cannot do as much damage to the next person in the way.
